blogs.title: When the Platelets Fall Too Soon: Early Post-Cardiac Surgery HIT From Preoperative Heparin Exposure
blogs.description: This post would examine the diagnostic trap of thrombocytopenia occurring before postoperative day 5 after cardiac surgery, a timeframe that often pushes clinicians away from HIT. Using this case, it would review how recent preoperative heparin exposure, even a relatively small dose during cardiac catheterization, can prime an early-onset HIT presentation. The piece would focus on timing patterns, interpretation of postoperative platelet trajectories after CPB, and how to distinguish expected surgical thrombocytopenia from pathologic immune-mediated decline.

blogs.title: Not Just HIT, but Autoimmune HIT: Recognizing the Severe Hypercoagulable Phenotype
blogs.description: This post would focus on autoimmune HIT as a distinct and more dangerous variant of HIT, emphasizing clues such as profound thrombocytopenia, thrombosis despite heparin discontinuation, and laboratory evidence of consumptive coagulopathy. It would discuss why a platelet nadir of 13×10^9/L, rising d-dimer, falling fibrinogen, and schistocytosis should raise concern for aHIT rather than routine postoperative thrombocytopenia or classic HIT. The broader teaching point would be when clinicians should escalate from 'possible HIT' to 'severe aHIT physiology.'

blogs.title: The Indeterminate SRA That Wasn’t: How to Read Unusual HIT Functional Assays
blogs.description: This post would unpack the laboratory teaching value of the case, especially the serotonin-release assay showing strong platelet activation at 0 heparin as well as low-dose heparin, with only partial inhibition by Fc receptor blockade. It would explain what a classic HIT assay pattern looks like, how aHIT alters that pattern, and why an atypical or 'indeterminate' functional assay should not automatically downgrade diagnostic confidence when the clinical picture is compelling. The post would also highlight the importance of close clinician-laboratory communication in complex HIT cases.

blogs.title: Argatroban, Fondaparinux, and IVIG: Managing aHIT When Standard Therapy Seems Inadequate
blogs.description: This post would explore the treatment tensions in severe autoimmune HIT after major surgery and ischemic stroke. It would discuss the rationale for initial argatroban use in a high-bleeding-risk patient, the addition of high-dose IVIG to interrupt Fc-mediated platelet activation, and the subsequent switch to therapeutic fondaparinux when hypercoagulability appeared to persist. The piece would use the case to review practical bedside decision-making when platelet counts do not rebound quickly and biomarkers suggest ongoing prothrombotic activity.

blogs.title: Delirium, Stroke, and HIT: Why Subtle Neurologic Change After Cardiac Surgery Deserves a Thrombotic Lens
blogs.description: This post would center on the neurologic complication in the case and the tendency to attribute postoperative mental status changes to routine delirium alone. It would argue that worsening delirium in a thrombocytopenic post-cardiac surgery patient should prompt consideration of HIT-associated arterial thrombosis, including ischemic stroke, even in the absence of focal deficits. More broadly, it would review the arterial thrombotic spectrum of HIT and how missed neurologic events can delay both diagnosis and treatment.

blogs.title: Beyond the Platelet Count: Using Fibrinogen, D-Dimer, and Smear Findings to Track HIT Activity
blogs.description: This post would highlight an underappreciated bedside strategy: following global markers of coagulation activation to assess disease trajectory in severe HIT. Using this case, it would show how falling fibrinogen, rising d-dimer, and the later appearance of schistocytes suggested ongoing consumptive coagulopathy despite anticoagulation. The post would discuss how these adjunctive data can help clinicians judge whether a patient is stabilizing, whether therapy may be insufficient, and when a diagnosis like aHIT better fits the overall picture.
